title: Fondant rose
subtitle: modelling a classic rose from fondant icing
excerpt: A fondant rose is built petal by petal from individually shaped pieces of fondant, assembled around a central cone. Unlike a piped buttercream rose, a fondant rose is modelled at room temperature over several minutes and can be made days ahead. The finished flower is rigid and holds its shape through storage, transport, and cutting. The method here covers a full open rose with five to seven visible petals.
sourceNotes: Fondant modelling for cake decoration has origins in the sugar-paste work of European pâtisserie and confectionery, documented in British sugarcraft from at least the 19th century. The fondant rose is the most widely taught sugarcraft flower and a standard unit in the City and Guilds Sugarcraft qualification. Commercially, moulded fondant flowers appeared on wedding cakes from the mid-20th century onward, displacing the older piped royal icing spray. The modelling technique is the same whether the material is rolled fondant, gum paste, or flower paste, the open-petal style used here is the quickest version that reads as a realistic rose rather than a stylised one.

recipe.batchNotes: Make the roses several days ahead and store in an airtight box lined with tissue paper at room temperature.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: Roses can be made up to a week ahead. They must be fully dry before placing on a cake.

content.text: A fondant rose is built up from a central cone around which petals are wrapped and overlapped. Each petal is thinned at the edge before attaching to give the curved, fluted look of a real petal. The finished rose needs at least 24 hours to dry completely before it's placed on a cake. Make several while you have the fondant out, the first one is always the least refined.

Roll a small piece of fondant (about 10 g) into a ball, then form it into a cone shape with a rounded top, this is the tight centre bud around which the petals wrap. The cone should be about 2 to 3 cm tall. Insert a cocktail stick into the base for handling. Set aside.

Pinch off pieces of fondant about 8 g each and roll each one into a ball, then flatten to a round disc about 3 mm thick. Lay each disc on the foam pad and run a ball tool around the upper half of the petal, pressing firmly to thin and slightly ruffle the edge. This gives a natural curl. Make three petals for the inner layer and four or five for the outer layer.

Wrap the first petal around the cone so the thinned edge stands above the cone tip. Press the base of the petal firmly to the cone to secure. Wrap the second petal opposite the first, tucking the edge under the previous petal at one side. Add the third inner petal, tucking one edge under and leaving one free. The three inner petals should form a tight, barely open bud.

Add four or five outer petals one at a time, positioning each between two inner petals and cupping them outward slightly so they open away from the centre. Press the base of each firmly and gently flute the top edge outward with a finger to emphasise the open shape. When complete, stand the rose upright on the cocktail stick stuck into a polystyrene block or a ball of fondant so the petals dry in a natural open position. Leave at room temperature for at least 24 hours.
